lines: How many people are in your family?
There are 4 people in my family: dad, mom, my older brother and me.
Do you have a younger sister?
No, I don't have a younger sister.

classifiers.title: 一个人, not just "one rén"
classifiers.body: In Chinese, a number almost never sits directly next to a noun — between the two comes a measure word (a kind of "unit word"). 个 (gè) is the most generic measure word, used for people and many other things.

classifiers.title: 个 (gè) or 口 (kǒu)?
classifiers.body: To count people in general, 个 does the job. But to count how many people live in the same household, Chinese has a specific measure word: kǒu (口, literally "mouth") — only in that family context.

you.title: 有 (yǒu) — "to have" / "there is"
you.body: 有 (yǒu) is the verb used both to say that someone has something and to say that something exists. Simple structure: Subject + 有 + Object.

he.title: 和 (hé) — joining nouns
he.body: 和 (hé) is like "and," but it only joins nouns to each other — never whole sentences. To connect two complete sentences, Chinese usually uses no linking word at all.

meiyou.title: 没(有) — negating "to have"
meiyou.body: To negate 有 (to have), Chinese doesn't use 不 — it uses 没 or 没有, specifically for this. It's one of the few exceptions to the general rule of negating with 不.
examples: I don't have a younger sister.

politica-filho-unico-historia.title: Why many people in the parents' generation have only one sibling (or none)
politica-filho-unico-historia.body: From 1979 until the end of 2015, China had the one-child policy (一孩政策), which limited most urban families to having just one child, as a way to curb population growth. The policy was officially ended in 2016, replaced first by permission to have two children and later three — but its effect still shows today in the structure of many Chinese families.
